Loop is one agent retrying. Graph is a team with handoff rules.

11 min read
1 hour ago

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

On July 18, OpenClaw’s author Peter Steinberger asked a question on X that landed harder than he probably expected: is everyone still talking about Loop, or has the conversation already moved to Graph?
Two days later, Codez published a long tutorial laying out a 14-step path to learning Graph Engineering from scratch.
I’m guessing your reaction was the same as mine: I haven’t even finished figuring out Loop. Now I’m supposed to draw diagrams?
Quick refresher, since everything below compares against it. Loop is the mechanism where a single agent checks and corrects itself over and over until the output clears the bar — write a draft, review it, redo it if it’s wrong, repeat until it passes.
I’m not going to march through 14 vocabulary words. Node, Edge, Schema, Router, Fan-out/Fan-in all show up below in plain language anyway. Here’s the version a normal person can act on:
Graph Engineering is dividing work among a group of agents, then specifying how work gets handed off, where it gets checked, and when to stop.
Start by treating your agent as a new hire
Say you hire someone to write you a daily AI news briefing.
The simplest approach is to hand them everything: find the news, read the sources, verify what’s true, pick the highlights, write the piece, fix the typos.
That’s the single agent everyone already knows. Your prompt is the job description. Loop is them proofreading their own draft and redoing it until it passes.
Simple tasks? Fine. But as the work piles up, this one hire starts drowning. They’re flipping through sources while trying to remember numbers while thinking about structure. The context fills up, and the stuff they read early gets forgotten fastest.
So Graph Engineering does the thing that sounds obvious the moment you say it out loud: stop making one person do all of this. Build a team.
Someone gathers material. Someone checks facts. Someone writes. Someone hunts for errors. Clear division of labor, one finished piece at the end.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

One clarification while we’re here, because the terms get mixed up constantly: Graph Reasoning and Graph Engineering are not the same thing. Graph Reasoning is about reasoning structure inside the model. Graph Engineering is about orchestrating multiple agents at the engineering layer. This article is about the second one.
Nodes are roles. Edges are handoff slips.
The two words that matter most in a graph are Node and Edge.

• A Node is a job: researcher, translator, fact-checker, writer, reviewer.

• An Edge says who passes work to whom — and exactly what gets passed.
Here’s the trap almost everyone falls into: things happening in order does not mean they depend on each other.
Say I ask an agent to summarize a document, then check the weather in Beijing. The weather lookup doesn’t need to wait for the summary. Both can start at the same instant.
That’s where a lot of agent setups bleed time. Everything gets written as A → B → C → D, and nothing downstream starts until the thing above it finishes.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

A cleaner example: B and C both need material from A, but C doesn’t need anything from B. So the moment A finishes, B and C can both launch. Making C sit in line behind B is pure waiting.
The most basic skill in Graph Engineering is seeing which dependencies are real — what genuinely has to wait, and what can start right now.
Once tasks can run in parallel, the question changes from who waits for whom to how do results get handed to the next agent.
Picture the researcher agent finishing its search and returning one big wall of text. The writing agent can’t find the source links and can’t tell which parts are facts and which are conclusions. So it guesses all over again.
The fix is a fixed format for every handoff. The researcher must return three things: headline, source link, importance. Miss one and the handoff fails. Only when all three are present does the writer proceed.
Technically that format rule is called a Schema. Think of it as a standardized handoff slip.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Now Node and Edge are easy: the Node defines what this agent is responsible for, the Edge defines which data it owes to whom. The clearer the handoff format, the less the next agent has to interpret.
Which means the genuinely hard part of multi-agent work isn’t the agents. It’s writing down every step’s deliverable, how it gets checked, and what happens when it fails — in advance.
Skip that, and more agents just means more rework.
The graph you’ll actually draw is a diamond
The most common graph shape is not complicated.
Split the task, let several agents work at once, pull the results back, dedupe and filter, then hand everything to one agent to produce the final output.
Take writing this article. One agent reads the original X thread. One agent digs through Anthropic’s official docs. A third looks at how people are actually discussing Graph Engineering. All three start simultaneously.
When the material comes back, duplicates get stripped, and the rest goes to the final drafter and reviewer — me. I never have to hold fifteen browser tabs in my head. I just receive the organized result.
That’s Fan-out and Fan-in. Fan-out distributes the work, Fan-in collects the results. Chain the two together and you get the diamond.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

But that collected material isn’t ready to write from. It might cite something stale, or treat somebody’s paraphrase as an official statement.
So the last agent runs an acceptance pass first: do the links open, do the numbers and dates line up, do any two sources contradict each other. Only then does it start writing.
That error-hunting role is the Reviewer or Verifier. Its job isn't to write another answer. It's to decide whether the previous answer can be trusted.
And ‘check it’ isn’t one fixed action — the intensity should scale with the stakes:

• An ordinary claim? One agent doing a fast pass is enough.

• Important data, a security question, a product conclusion? Several agents cross-checking from different angles.
The role that decides which checking path a given item takes is the Router. It's triage: it reads the risk level and sends the task down a different edge.
If the research agent claims something is officially confirmed, the verifier has to locate the primary source. If all it can find is press coverage, that claim gets downgraded — or sent back to be researched again. Only what survives the check makes it into the article.
Two more things this shape needs:
Isolation, if the agents write code instead of gathering facts. Give each one its own workspace (a git worktree, for instance). Otherwise two agents editing the same file means whoever saves second silently erases the first one’s work.
A stop condition, if checking loops back. Rejected work returning to the research stage and getting re-checked creates a cycle — and a cycle needs a documented exit, like stop after two consecutive rounds find nothing new. Without it you’re the boss who keeps yelling ‘check it again,’ and your agents will keep working while the token meter runs.
Strip away the vocabulary and the whole pipeline is this: someone finds material, someone organizes it, someone checks it. Fails go back. Only what passes becomes the conclusion.
Two receipts, so this stops being theory
Fair question at this point: does any of this actually pay off, or does it just look tidy on a whiteboard?
Receipt one — Anthropic measured it on their own research system. They wired up exactly the shape described above: a lead agent that scopes the question, subagents that search in parallel, results merged back. With Claude Opus 4 as the lead and Claude Sonnet 4 as the subagents, that system beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research eval.
Then the same writeup gives you the invoice: agents use roughly 4× the tokens of a chat, and multi-agent systems about 15×. They also found token usage alone explains 80% of the performance variance they measured. That is Bill 01 from the next section, stated by the people who paid it.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Receipt two — Uber shipped a graph, not a diagram. Their developer platform team built AutoCover on LangGraph: domain-expert agents that scaffold, generate, and execute unit tests, running in parallel, with results streaming into your IDE as each branch finishes. You right-click a file and watch tests appear. At GitHub Universe the team put the number at around 21,000 developer hours saved across roughly 5,000 engineers.
Notice what that is, structurally. It’s the diamond. Fan-out across independent test targets, execute in isolated workspaces, fan back in. Nothing exotic — just the arrows drawn honestly.
And notice the boundary Anthropic drew on themselves, because it’s the most useful sentence in their whole post: multi-agent is poorly suited to domains where every agent needs the same context, or where agents depend heavily on each other — and coding parallelizes less than research does. The people with the strongest possible incentive to sell you on agent swarms published the limit anyway.
Three bills you still have to do the math on
Everything above is about splitting work across agents. Here’s what that section conveniently ignores: every agent you start has to read material, think, and produce output. All of that burns tokens.
Summoning ten frontier models to research one article probably does cover more ground than one model. It also costs ten times as much. Parallelism buys you wall-clock time. It does not make those ten experts work for free.
The way to control that is to stop sending every job to the most expensive model. Pulling headlines, formatting, simple classification — cheap model. Judging whether something is true, resolving conflicts, forming the final conclusion — strong model.
Think of it as a newsroom: the editor-in-chief doesn’t need to personally sort the clippings. You bring them in for the call that actually matters.
Then there’s scheduling, which affects speed independently of model choice:

• Barrier: ten sources have to be deduped together, so you wait for all ten agents to return before anything moves. Like a meeting — nothing starts until everyone’s in the room.

• Pipeline: each source can be processed alone, so nothing waits. The first one back gets checked immediately, the second one back gets processed next. Like an assembly line.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

So designing an agent graph really comes down to three numbers: how many agents you start, which model each one runs, and which steps genuinely have to wait for each other.
A good graph finishes the task faster and cheaper. A bad graph just gets more models burning tokens in parallel.
Claude Code will now draw the graph for you
By now you’ve probably spotted the catch: a graph lets multiple agents work together, but somebody still has to design the graph.
Who researches, who verifies, what can start at once, what has to wait, who makes the final call — historically the developer wrote all of that up front.
Claude Code’s Dynamic Workflows hands that job to Claude too. You state the end goal. Claude analyzes the task and generates a JavaScript orchestration script.
For the article example, it can dispatch agents to hunt the original thread, the official docs, and outside discussion; run plain code to dedupe when the material returns; send a verifier to check the sources; and hand the survivors to a writing agent.
In Claude Code you can ask for a Workflow directly, or run /deep-research. Turn on ultracode and Claude will first judge whether the task is even complex enough to justify spinning up a squad.
